questions.question: Explain what two-state signals and logic gates are, how gates are built in this term and in real equipment, and why gates matter for control.
questions.expected_answer: Logic handles signals with only two states, a switch open or closed, a lamp off or on, a sensor no or yes, a wire low or high, labelled 0 and 1, off and on, or false and true interchangeably. A logic gate has one or more two-state inputs and one two-state output with a rule that fixes the output for every combination of inputs, obeying it instantly and identically every time. This term gates are built from switches as inputs and a lamp as output, while real gates are millions of transistors on a chip following the same rules; one switch and a lamp is the simplest gate with output equal to input, two or more inputs give the AND and OR gates, and NOT follows in Grade 9. Gates matter because every control decision is built from them: a machine requiring two conditions is an AND, an alarm triggered by any sensor is an OR, and traffic lights, washing machine programmes and bank card checks are stacks of both, so seeing the gate in a machine enables the design of safe machines such as the panic button.

questions.question: State the AND rule, describe the series-switch AND circuit and its four test results, draw or describe the symbol, and give everyday uses with the design reasoning.
questions.expected_answer: An AND gate's output is 1 only when every input is 1; with inputs A and B the output is on only when both are on and off if either or both are off. It is built with two switches in series with a lamp and a cell, so current reaches the lamp only when both switches are closed on the single path; testing gives both open dark, A only dark, B only dark, both closed lit, one lit combination of four. The symbol is a D shape, flat on the input side with two lines entering and rounded on the output side with one line leaving, read as output on when A AND B are on. Uses are safety interlocks and double conditions: a microwave heats when the door is closed AND start is pressed, a car starts when the key is turned AND the clutch is pressed or the lever is in park, a lift moves when doors are closed AND a floor is selected, an ATM pays when the card is valid AND the PIN is correct, and a guillotine cuts only when both hands press separate buttons so no hand is under the blade. AND demands more before acting, guarding dangerous or costly actions, and if one input fails off the system refuses to work, which is annoying but safe.

questions.question: State the OR rule, describe the parallel-switch OR circuit and its test results, draw or describe the symbol, give everyday uses, and compare AND with OR.
questions.expected_answer: An OR gate's output is 1 when any input is 1 and 0 only when all inputs are 0; with inputs A and B the output is on if A or B or both are on and off only when both are off. It is built with two switches in parallel feeding a lamp, giving two paths so either closed switch lights the lamp and both must be open to darken it; testing gives both open dark, A only lit, B only lit, both lit, three lit combinations of four. The symbol is a curved shield or arrowhead with a concave input side where two lines enter and a pointed output with one line leaving, read as output on when A OR B is on, where OR includes both. Uses are alarms and multiple triggers: a burglar alarm sounds if the door OR a window OR a movement sensor triggers, a car's interior light comes on if any door opens, a fire alarm sounds if any detector fires, a microwave stops if the door opens OR the timer ends, a nurse is called if any patient presses a button, and a panic button alarm sounds if any of several buttons is pressed; OR acts on the first sign of trouble, suiting alarms, with false alarms as its weakness. AND is series switches that demand everything and guard actions; OR is parallel switches that accept anything and raise alarms; real systems combine them, as the microwave runs on door closed AND start and stops on door open OR timer done.
